error_modes.label: Airspeed matching with the leader during roll and initial climb

texts.0: SP, due to coarse and delayed throttle handling after the leader advanced power, did not stabilize the airspeed on the leader's flown value during the roll and the initial climb. Airspeed diverged by up to 28 knots, the aircraft accelerated forward of the leader's wing line and the fore-aft position could no longer be regained with power alone. IP took the throttle and repositioned the aircraft aft of the leader to prevent an overshoot ahead of lead.
texts.1: SP, due to power changes applied in large steps instead of small anticipated corrections, did not hold the airspeed matched to the leader through the acceleration and the initial climb. The divergence reached about 20 knots, at the limit of the tolerance, and was arrested only after two verbal prompts from the IP on the throttle position. The aircraft returned to the briefed airspeed with a noticeable delay after each prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late power reduction once the leader stabilized the climb speed, did not match the leader's airspeed immediately after the gear and flap retraction. Airspeed diverged by about 14 knots and the aircraft crept forward of the briefed fore-aft position. SP recognized the trend on the leader's wing line, reduced power in small increments and re-established the matched airspeed within a few seconds, without any intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated the leader's power settings and matched the airspeed accurately through the roll, the acceleration and the initial climb. Airspeed remained within 10 knots of the leader's flown value at all times and the fore-aft position stayed on the briefed reference. Power corrections were small, early and applied in the correct direction.
texts.4: SP matched the leader's airspeed with negligible deviations throughout the take off roll and the departure, holding the fore-aft reference essentially fixed. Power corrections were anticipatory and so small that no airspeed excursion developed at any point, including the configuration change. The matched airspeed was maintained without any prompting or assistance.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed matched to the leader within standards, but consistently on the fast side, with deviations repeatedly reaching 9 to 10 knots after each power change. The pattern shows a tendency to add power before assessing the leader's acceleration and then to chase the resulting overshoot. SP is expected to reduce the size of the power corrections and to anticipate the leader's setting so that the airspeed spread stays well inside the tolerance.

texts_at.1: SP held the airspeed matched to the leader with the divergence reaching about 20 knots, at the tolerance limit, because the power changes were applied in large steps instead of small anticipated corrections. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the leader's power settings so the divergence does not run to the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP let the airspeed diverge about 14 knots from the leader's value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the power reduction after the leader stabilized was made a beat late. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power as the leader stabilizes rather than a beat afterward.
texts_at.3: SP held the airspeed within 10 knots of the leader's value through the roll and the initial climb on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after a power setting held a touch late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate power on every departure with the same lead the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP let the airspeed diverge toward 14 knots from the leader's value but recognized the trend on the leader's wing line and reduced power in small increments without prompting, re-establishing the matched airspeed within a few seconds. Anticipating the leader's power settings, rather than correcting the divergence afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good airspeed matching with the leader.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the leader's power settings and matched the airspeed accurately through the roll, the acceleration and the initial climb, holding the airspeed within 10 knots of the leader's value with power corrections small and applied in the correct direction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good airspeed matching with the leader.
texts_above.4: SP matched the leader's airspeed with negligible deviations throughout the takeoff roll and the departure, holding the fore-aft reference essentially fixed with anticipatory power corrections. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent airspeed matching with the leader.

error_modes.label: Vertical position and altitude control during the departure segment

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check between the leader's wing line and the altimeter after the configuration change, did not maintain the briefed vertical position during the initial climb. The aircraft ended up more than 350 feet off the leader's altitude, well outside the tolerance, and the vertical stack became irrecoverable from that geometry. IP took control and repositioned the aircraft into the briefed vertical reference before continuing the departure.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the leader's fuselage without any reference to the vertical stack cues, did not maintain the vertical position during the climb out. The altitude split reached about 300 feet, at the limit of the tolerance, and was reduced only after repeated verbal directions from the IP. Each correction was initiated late and the vertical reference was regained slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that lapsed briefly while the gear and flaps were being retracted, did not hold the briefed vertical position immediately after the configuration change. The altitude split grew to about 200 feet above the leader. SP re-established the reference on the leader's canopy line, corrected with a small pitch adjustment and returned to the briefed stack within a few seconds, with no intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained an accurate vertical position on the leader through the lift off, the configuration change and the initial climb. The altitude split remained within 150 feet at all times and the briefed stack was held without oscillation. Pitch corrections were small, timely and referenced to the correct visual cues on the leader.
texts.4: SP held the vertical position on the leader with negligible deviations from lift off through the departure, keeping the stack visually fixed. The altitude split remained within a few tens of feet even during the configuration change, when the vertical reference is most easily lost. Corrections were anticipatory and no vertical excursion developed at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the vertical position within standards, but with a repeated tendency to settle low on the leader, with the split reaching 130 to 150 feet after each pitch change. The pattern indicates that the cross-check returns to the leader's line later than required once a cockpit task is introduced. SP is expected to re-establish the visual reference immediately after each configuration action so that the vertical stack stays close to the briefed value.

texts_at.1: SP held the vertical split at about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, because attention stayed on the leader's fuselage with no reference to the vertical stack cues until IP directed the correction repeatedly. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the vertical stack reference continuously rather than needing repeated direction to regain it.
texts_at.2: SP let the vertical split grow to about 200 feet above the leader, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the cross-check lapsed briefly while the gear and flaps were being retracted. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the vertical reference through the configuration change rather than letting the cross-check lapse.
texts_at.3: SP held the vertical split within 150 feet through the configuration change and the initial climb on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after the reference was regained a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the reference through that one configuration change as well as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP let the vertical split grow toward 200 feet above the leader during the configuration change but re-established the reference on the leader's canopy line without prompting, correcting with a small pitch adjustment. Holding the vertical reference through the configuration change, rather than letting the cross-check lapse, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid vertical position control on the departure.
texts_above.3: SP maintained an accurate vertical position on the leader through the lift off, the configuration change and the initial climb, holding the split within 150 feet with pitch corrections small, timely and referenced to the correct visual cues. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate vertical position control on the departure.
texts_above.4: SP held the vertical position on the leader with negligible deviations from lift off through the departure, keeping the stack visually fixed even during the configuration change, when the reference is most easily lost. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary vertical position control on the departure.

error_modes.label: Runway and departure heading tracking as number two

texts.0: SP, due to rudder inputs applied late and in the wrong direction during the acceleration, did not track the leader's heading through the roll and the initial turn out. The heading split exceeded 12 deg, the aircraft diverged laterally from the briefed line and the lateral spacing opened well beyond the briefed distance. IP took control to re-establish the heading and to close the aircraft back onto the leader's departure track.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient anticipation of the swing during the power application, did not hold the leader's heading through the roll and the initial climb out. The heading split reached about 10 deg, at the limit of the tolerance, and was corrected only after verbal heading calls from the IP. The aircraft was returned to the leader's track late and with an overshoot in the opposite direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly delayed rudder correction as the aircraft accelerated, did not track the leader's heading precisely during the take off roll. The heading split grew to about 7 deg with a visible lateral drift away from the leader. SP identified the divergence, applied a coordinated rudder correction and re-established the leader's track promptly, without prompting.
texts.3: SP tracked the leader's heading accurately from brake release through the initial climb, holding the heading split within 5 deg at all times. The lateral line on the leader remained on the briefed reference through the acceleration and the turn out. Rudder inputs were small, coordinated and applied without delay.
texts.4: SP tracked the leader's heading with negligible deviations throughout the roll and the departure, holding the lateral reference visually fixed. The heading split stayed within a couple of degrees even during the power application and the turn out. Directional control was continuous and required no correction beyond minimal rudder pressure.
texts.marginal: SP tracked the leader's heading within standards, but the split repeatedly grew to 4 to 5 deg before being corrected, always toward the same side. The trend shows that the directional correction is applied after the divergence has become visible rather than at its onset. SP is expected to anticipate the directional tendency during the power application so that the heading split remains well inside the tolerance.

texts_at.1: SP held the heading split to about 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, because the anticipation of the swing during power application was insufficient until IP made verbal heading calls. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the swing at power application so the correction does not depend on a heading call.
texts_at.2: SP let the heading split grow to about 7 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the rudder correction as the aircraft accelerated was slightly delayed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the rudder correction as the swing begins rather than after the drift is visible.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the leader's heading within 5 degrees from brake release through the initial climb on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after a rudder input applied a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold that same tracking on every departure that the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP let the heading split grow toward 7 degrees with a visible lateral drift away from the leader but identified the divergence and applied a coordinated rudder correction without prompting, re-establishing the leader's track promptly. Applying the rudder correction as the swing begins, rather than after the drift is visible, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady heading tracking on the departure roll.
texts_above.3: SP tracked the leader's heading accurately from brake release through the initial climb, holding the split within 5 degrees with the lateral line on the leader remaining on the briefed reference throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined heading tracking on the departure roll.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the leader's heading with negligible deviations throughout the roll and the departure, holding the lateral reference visually fixed even during the power application and the turn out. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate heading tracking on the departure roll.

error_modes.label: Line up checks and notification to the formation leader

texts.0: SP, due to a checklist not followed correctly (AE102) before brake release, did not complete the line up checks and did not inform the formation leader that the aircraft was ready. Two items of the check remained unactioned and the omission was still present when the leader signalled the power application, so the aircraft entered the roll in an incorrect configuration. IP stopped the sequence, directed the checks to be completed on the runway and informed the leader before the take off could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to an item of the line up checks omitted under the workload of taxiing into position, did not execute the checks without mistakes and did not report ready to the leader in time. The omission was identified and corrected only after the IP prompted the item by name, and the ready call reached the leader after the leader had already queried the flight. The sequence continued only once the check was completed on verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to the attention required to establish the line up position on the leader, did not complete the line up checks in the briefed order and delayed the ready call. SP identified the omitted item without being told, actioned it and passed the ready call to the leader with a delay of only a few seconds, before the leader initiated the take off signal. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP executed the line up checks accurately and in the briefed order, with no omitted or mis-set item, and informed the formation leader promptly that the aircraft was ready. The checks were completed while the correct line up position on the leader was maintained. The ready call was made with standard phraseology and at the correct moment in the sequence.
texts.4: SP completed the line up checks without a single error and with time in hand, while holding an accurate line up position on the leader. The ready call was passed to the leader immediately on completion, using standard phraseology and without any dead time in the sequence. Cockpit tasks and the visual reference on the leader were managed in parallel with no degradation of either.
texts.marginal: SP executed the line up checks without errors and informed the leader, but the checks were completed close to the point at which the leader expected the ready call, leaving no margin in the sequence. The pattern shows that cockpit actions are started only after the line up position has been fully stabilized rather than in parallel with it. SP is expected to begin the checks earlier so that the ready call is passed to the leader with a comfortable margin.

texts_at.1: SP passed the ready call to the leader only after the leader queried the flight, having omitted an item of the line up checks under the workload of taxiing into position. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the checks and pass the ready call before the leader needs to ask for it.
texts_at.2: SP delayed the line up checks and the ready call while establishing position on the leader, then identified the omitted item without being told and passed the ready call with only a few seconds' delay before the leader's takeoff signal. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to run the checks and hold the line up position together rather than delaying the checks until position is settled.
texts_at.3: SP executed the line up checks accurately and informed the leader promptly that the aircraft was ready on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth ready call arriving a few seconds later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to pass that one call as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP delayed the line up checks while establishing position on the leader but identified the omitted item without being told, actioning it and passing the ready call with only a few seconds' delay before the leader's takeoff signal. Running the checks and holding the line up position together, rather than delaying the checks until position is settled, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable line-up check discipline as wingman.
texts_above.3: SP executed the line up checks accurately and in the briefed order, with no omitted or mis-set item, informing the formation leader promptly that the aircraft was ready while holding the correct line up position on the leader. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good line-up check discipline as wingman.
texts_above.4: SP completed the line up checks without a single error and with time in hand, while holding an accurate line up position on the leader and passing the ready call immediately on completion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior line-up check discipline as wingman.

error_modes.label: Position keeping relative to the leader during the take off roll

texts.0: SP, due to power set well above the setting required to hold the briefed position, did not keep the proper position relative to the leader during the take off roll. The aircraft moved forward of the leader's wing line by more than a full fuselage length and the lateral spacing closed at the same time. IP took control on the runway to arrest the closure and to re-establish safe spacing from the leader before lift off.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections made in large steps rather than by small continuous adjustments, did not keep the proper position during the take off roll. The aircraft oscillated fore and aft around the briefed reference through most of the roll and reached the limit of the acceptable position band. Position was recovered on each occasion only after verbal corrections from the IP, and the reference was never fully stabilized before rotation.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late power adjustment as the leader accelerated, did not hold the briefed position during the first part of the take off roll. The aircraft drifted aft of the leader's wing line by about half a fuselage length. SP recognized the divergence against the leader's canopy reference, corrected with a measured power increase and re-established the position well before rotation, without any assistance.
texts.3: SP kept the proper position relative to the leader throughout the take off roll, holding the briefed fore-aft and lateral references from brake release to lift off. Power was managed continuously in small increments so that no position excursion developed during the acceleration. The transition to flight was made with the position reference unchanged.
texts.4: SP held the briefed position on the leader through the entire take off roll with negligible variation, keeping the visual references essentially locked. Power was anticipated rather than chased, so the acceleration and the lift off produced no perceptible movement in the formation geometry. The position was maintained with no prompting of any kind.
texts.marginal: SP kept the proper position during the take off roll within acceptable limits, but tended to sit consistently aft of the briefed reference and to close the gap only in the final part of the roll. The trend suggests that power is set conservatively at brake release and adjusted only once the divergence has become obvious. SP is expected to match the leader's acceleration from the start so that the position reference is held steady throughout the roll.

texts_at.1: SP oscillated fore and aft around the briefed reference for most of the roll, reaching the limit of the acceptable position band each time before IP's verbal correction restored it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the reference with small continuous power adjustments rather than needing it restored by verbal correction each time.
texts_at.2: SP drifted aft of the leader's wing line by about half a fuselage length after a slightly late power adjustment as the leader accelerated, then recognized the divergence against the leader's canopy reference and corrected with a measured power increase without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to match the leader's acceleration from the start rather than correcting a drift once it is visible.
texts_at.3: SP kept the proper position relative to the leader through the takeoff roll on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after a power adjustment made a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to match the leader's acceleration on that one departure as closely as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP drifted aft of the leader's wing line by about half a fuselage length after a slightly late power adjustment but recognized the divergence against the leader's canopy reference and corrected with a measured power increase without prompting, well before rotation. Matching the leader's acceleration from the start, rather than correcting a drift once it is visible, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured position keeping during the takeoff roll.
texts_above.3: SP kept the proper position relative to the leader throughout the takeoff roll, holding the briefed fore-aft and lateral references from brake release to lift off with power managed continuously in small increments. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise position keeping during the takeoff roll.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed position on the leader through the entire takeoff roll with negligible variation, keeping the visual references essentially locked as power was anticipated rather than chased. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate position keeping during the takeoff roll.

error_modes.label: Timely notification to the leader when the position cannot be held

texts.0: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in stating unable when the briefed position could no longer be held, did not inform the leader timely that the aircraft was out of position. The aircraft continued the roll well outside the position band with no transmission, and the leader remained unaware of the wingman's state through rotation. IP made the call to the leader and took control to re-establish safe spacing.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in transmitting a deviation that could be read as an admission of poor performance, did not inform the leader timely when the position degraded during the roll. The call was made only after the IP directed it, by which time the aircraft had reached the limit of the acceptable position band. The leader's response was consequently late relative to the developing geometry.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief hesitation over the wording of the transmission, did not inform the leader immediately when the position began to degrade during the roll. The aircraft was displaced from the briefed reference for several seconds before the call was made. SP then transmitted a clear and correct statement of the position on his own initiative, in time for the leader to act, with no intervention required.
texts.3: SP informed the leader timely and in plain language as soon as the briefed position could not be held, stating the actual position of the aircraft. The transmission was made without hesitation and allowed the leader to adjust the sequence in good time. Standard phraseology was used throughout.
texts.4: SP monitored the developing position continuously and informed the leader at the first indication that the briefed reference was at risk, before any significant displacement occurred. The transmission was concise, unambiguous and gave the leader the full picture of the wingman's state. The exchange did not interrupt the SP's control of the aircraft or of the visual reference.
texts.marginal: SP informed the leader when the position could not be held, and the call was made within an acceptable time, but only after the displacement had become clearly visible rather than at its onset. The pattern indicates a reluctance to transmit until the deviation is beyond doubt. SP is expected to make the call at the first recognized trend, so that the leader has the maximum time available to respond.

texts_at.1: SP informed the leader only after IP directed the call, by which time the aircraft had reached the limit of the acceptable position band, because stating a deviation was hesitated over as an admission of poor performance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make the call as soon as the position degrades rather than needing it directed.
texts_at.2: SP was displaced from the briefed reference for several seconds before transmitting because of a brief hesitation over the wording, then made a clear and correct statement of the position without prompting, in time for the leader to act. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to transmit the moment the position begins to degrade rather than after several seconds of hesitation.
texts_at.3: SP informed the leader timely and in plain language as soon as the briefed position could not be held on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth call coming a few seconds later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that one call as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP hesitated briefly over the wording before transmitting, leaving the aircraft displaced from the briefed reference for several seconds, but then transmitted a clear and correct statement of the position without prompting, in time for the leader to act. Transmitting the moment the position begins to degrade, rather than after several seconds of hesitation, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent assertiveness in reporting the position.
texts_above.3: SP informed the leader timely and in plain language as soon as the briefed position could not be held, stating the actual position without hesitation and using standard phraseology throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed assertiveness in reporting the position.
texts_above.4: SP monitored the developing position continuously and informed the leader at the first indication that the briefed reference was at risk, before any significant displacement occurred, with the transmission concise and unambiguous. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding assertiveness in reporting the position.

error_modes.label: Response to the leader's signals and cleaning up the aircraft configuration

texts.0: SP, due to a visual scan concentrated on the leader's wing tip rather than on the signalling area, did not follow the leader's signals and did not clean up the aircraft configuration as directed. The gear remained extended well past the leader's signal and the flap selection was made only after a direct order from the rear cockpit. IP took control of the configuration to bring the aircraft into the formation state before the departure turn.
texts.1: SP, due to the signal being read late while the aircraft was being repositioned, did not follow the leader's signals and did not clean the configuration in the briefed sequence. Gear and flap retraction lagged the leader's signal by several seconds and were completed only after verbal prompting from the IP. The formation reached the departure turn with the configuration change still being finalized.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary delay in reacquiring the leader's signalling reference after lift off, did not action the configuration change at the moment of the signal. Gear retraction was initiated about two seconds late and the flaps followed shortly after. SP identified the lag without prompting, completed the sequence correctly and had the aircraft clean well before the departure turn.
texts.3: SP followed the leader's signals accurately and cleaned the aircraft configuration in the briefed sequence and at the correct moment. Gear and flaps were retracted immediately on the leader's signal, with the visual reference on the leader maintained throughout the action. No signal was missed or misread.
texts.4: SP read every signal from the leader immediately and cleaned the configuration in the briefed sequence with no perceptible lag, while holding the formation position unchanged. The cockpit actions were completed without any degradation of the visual reference or of the aircraft path. The whole configuration change was completed as a single continuous and unhurried sequence.
texts.marginal: SP followed the leader's signals and cleaned the configuration within acceptable limits, but each action was initiated only after a visible pause to confirm the signal. The trend shows that the signalling reference is being reacquired rather than continuously monitored. SP is expected to keep the signalling area within the scan so that the configuration change follows the leader's signal without delay.

texts_at.1: SP completed gear and flap retraction several seconds behind the leader's signal and only after verbal prompting from IP, because the signal was read late while the aircraft was being repositioned. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read the leader's signal without delay rather than needing it prompted.
texts_at.2: SP initiated gear retraction about two seconds after the leader's signal because the signalling reference was reacquired late after lift off, then identified the lag without prompting and completed the sequence correctly well before the departure turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the signalling reference in the scan continuously rather than reacquiring it after lift off.
texts_at.3: SP followed the leader's signals accurately and cleaned the configuration in the briefed sequence on three of the four departures, the fourth showing a lag of a couple of seconds before the signal was read. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to read that one signal as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP initiated gear retraction about two seconds after the leader's signal because the signalling reference was reacquired late after lift off, but identified the lag without prompting and completed the sequence correctly well before the departure turn. Keeping the signalling reference in the scan continuously, rather than reacquiring it after lift off, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable response to the leader's configuration signals.
texts_above.3: SP followed the leader's signals accurately and cleaned the aircraft configuration in the briefed sequence and at the correct moment, with the visual reference on the leader maintained throughout and no signal missed or misread. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good response to the leader's configuration signals.
texts_above.4: SP read every signal from the leader immediately and cleaned the configuration in the briefed sequence with no perceptible lag, holding the formation position unchanged throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior response to the leader's configuration signals.

error_modes.label: Smoothness of control inputs and formation stability

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs made in large corrective movements instead of continuous small pressures, did not have smooth control of the aircraft during the roll and the initial climb. The aircraft oscillated in roll and pitch against the leader with an increasing amplitude, and the closure rate toward the leader became unpredictable. IP took control to damp the oscillation and to re-establish a stable formation geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to overcontrolling in roll while chasing the lateral reference, did not fly the aircraft smoothly during the departure. Each correction produced an overshoot in the opposite direction and the formation position was never stabilized without further input. The oscillation was damped only after repeated verbal direction on control pressures from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to corrections applied slightly larger than required after the configuration change, did not hold fully smooth control through the initial climb. Small pitch and roll oscillations developed against the leader's reference for a few seconds. SP reduced the size of the inputs on his own initiative, damped the oscillation and flew the remainder of the departure smoothly, without intervention.
texts.3: SP had smooth control of the aircraft throughout the formation take off, correcting with small continuous pressures rather than discrete inputs. The formation geometry remained stable through the acceleration, the lift off and the configuration change. No oscillation developed at any point in the sequence.
texts.4: SP flew the aircraft with consistently smooth and anticipatory control inputs, so that the formation position appeared static to the leader throughout the take off and departure. Corrections were made at the onset of each trend and were small enough to be imperceptible in the formation geometry. The aircraft was flown with no oscillation and no overcorrection at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP had smooth control of the aircraft within standards, but the corrections were slightly larger than required and produced a low-amplitude oscillation after each configuration change. The trend shows that inputs are made in response to a visible displacement rather than to the initial rate. SP is expected to correct earlier and with smaller pressures so that the formation position remains steady without any residual oscillation.

texts_at.1: SP produced an overshoot in the opposite direction on each correction while chasing the lateral reference, and the oscillation was damped only after repeated verbal direction on control pressures from IP. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to correct with continuous small pressures rather than discrete inputs that need to be damped afterward.
texts_at.2: SP let small pitch and roll oscillations develop against the leader's reference for a few seconds after the configuration change, because the corrections applied were slightly larger than required, then reduced the size of the inputs without prompting and damped the oscillation. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the corrections correctly from the first input rather than reducing them after an oscillation develops.
texts_at.3: SP had smooth control of the aircraft through the takeoff and departure on three of the four sorties, the fourth showing a brief oscillation after the configuration change before it was damped. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same smooth control on every sortie that the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP let small pitch and roll oscillations develop against the leader's reference for a few seconds after the configuration change but recognized this and reduced the size of the inputs without prompting, damping the oscillation and flying the remainder of the departure smoothly. Sizing the corrections correctly from the first input, rather than reducing them after an oscillation develops, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured smoothness of control during the departure.
texts_above.3: SP had smooth control of the aircraft throughout the formation takeoff, correcting with small continuous pressures rather than discrete inputs so the formation geometry remained stable through the acceleration, the lift off and the configuration change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise smoothness of control during the departure.
texts_above.4: SP flew the aircraft with consistently smooth and anticipatory control inputs, so the formation position appeared static to the leader throughout the takeoff and departure with no oscillation at any stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate smoothness of control during the departure.

error_modes.label: Drift, crosswind correction and lateral clearance from the leader

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured entirely by the leader's wing tip at the expense of the lateral drift picture, did not apply the correction required for the crosswind during the take off roll. The aircraft drifted toward the leader and the lateral spacing reduced to less than the briefed minimum while the closure continued unchecked. IP took control to arrest the drift and to restore lateral clearance from the leader.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan locked on a single point of the leader's airframe, did not correct the drift produced by the crosswind during the roll and the initial climb. Lateral spacing degraded to the minimum acceptable value and was restored only after direct verbal direction from the IP. The correction was applied late and the aircraft required a further input to stabilize the lateral reference.
texts.2: SP, due to the scan remaining on the leader's canopy for longer than required after lift off, did not correct the developing drift immediately. The lateral spacing reduced noticeably below the briefed reference before the trend was recognized. SP widened the scan, applied a coordinated correction into the wind and restored the briefed lateral spacing without prompting or intervention.
texts.3: SP applied the drift correction required by the crosswind from brake release onward and maintained the briefed lateral spacing from the leader throughout the take off and the initial climb. The scan covered the leader's reference, the runway environment and the aircraft path without fixation. Lateral clearance was never in question at any point.
texts.4: SP anticipated the crosswind effect and held the briefed lateral spacing from the leader with negligible variation through the roll, the lift off and the departure. The scan was distributed continuously across the leader's reference and the external picture, so no drift was allowed to develop. Lateral clearance remained constant and required no corrective action.
texts.marginal: SP corrected for the crosswind and maintained lateral spacing within standards, but the spacing repeatedly reduced toward the lower end of the briefed band before the correction was applied. The pattern shows a scan that dwells on the leader longer than necessary before returning to the drift cues. SP is expected to distribute the scan more evenly so that the lateral spacing is held steady rather than recovered.

texts_at.1: SP restored lateral clearance only after direct verbal direction from IP, because the scan was locked on a single point of the leader's airframe through the roll and the initial climb. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to widen the scan to include the drift cues so the correction does not need to be directed.
texts_at.2: SP let the lateral spacing reduce noticeably below the briefed reference because the scan remained on the leader's canopy longer than required after lift off, then widened the scan and applied a coordinated correction into the wind without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the scan moving between the leader and the drift cues rather than dwelling on the leader.
texts_at.3: SP applied the drift correction required by the crosswind and maintained the briefed lateral spacing on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after the scan dwelled on the leader a moment longer than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to distribute that one scan as evenly as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP let the lateral spacing reduce noticeably below the briefed reference because the scan remained on the leader's canopy longer than required after lift off, but widened the scan and applied a coordinated correction into the wind without prompting, restoring the briefed spacing. Keeping the scan moving between the leader and the drift cues, rather than dwelling on the leader, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent crosswind and lateral clearance discipline.
texts_above.3: SP applied the drift correction required by the crosswind from brake release onward and maintained the briefed lateral spacing throughout the takeoff and the initial climb, with the scan covering the leader's reference, the runway environment and the aircraft path without fixation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed crosswind and lateral clearance discipline.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the crosswind effect and held the briefed lateral spacing from the leader with negligible variation through the roll, the lift off and the departure, with the scan distributed continuously so no drift was allowed to develop. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding crosswind and lateral clearance discipline.

error_modes.label: Lineup on the close (fingertip) formation line and minimum wingtip clearance

texts.0: SP, due to taxiing into the run-up position by reference to the runway markings instead of establishing the close (fingertip) formation line on Number 1, did not set the briefed lineup geometry on his half of the runway and left clearly less than the minimum 20 feet of lateral wingtip clearance. The aircraft was also stopped abeam Number 1 rather than in the fore-aft position that Number 1 had taxied forward to allow, so the wingtips overlapped with no margin for the roll. IP took control on the runway and repositioned the aircraft on the formation line before the run-up signal was given.
texts.1: SP, due to a lineup reference taken on Number 1's nose rather than on the fingertip line, did not establish the briefed lateral spacing as the aircraft was brought into position. The wingtip clearance ended at about the 20 feet minimum, at the limit of what is acceptable, and was opened only after repeated verbal directions from the IP on the remaining offset. The head nod signifying ready for run-up was consequently given late.
texts.2: SP, due to stopping the aircraft on the first position that looked correct instead of confirming the fingertip line, did not set the briefed lateral spacing at the first attempt and ended slightly close on Number 1. SP recognized the tight wingtip clearance before signalling ready, taxied out a few feet and re-established the formation line with a clear margin over the 20 feet minimum. The lineup was completed without any assistance.
texts.3: SP lined up on the close (fingertip) formation line on his own half of the runway, with lateral wingtip clearance comfortably above the 20 feet minimum and with the fore-aft position matched to the room Number 1 had left. The aircraft was stopped straight and aligned with the runway before the head nod was given. The geometry needed no adjustment afterwards.
texts.4: SP established the lineup geometry accurately at the first attempt, holding the fingertip line with clearly more than the minimum 20 feet of wingtip clearance and stopping in the exact fore-aft position allowed by Number 1's taxi distance. The aircraft was stopped straight on its own half of the runway and the head nod was given only once the position had been confirmed correct. No repositioning of any kind was required.
texts.marginal: SP lined up on the fingertip line with the wingtip clearance within limits, but consistently close to the 20 feet minimum and with the aircraft slightly forward of the position Number 1 had allowed. The trend is toward accepting the first position reached rather than confirming the formation line before stopping. SP is expected to build in a margin over the minimum clearance so that a small lateral drift during the roll does not erode it.

texts_at.1: SP opened the wingtip clearance only after repeated verbal directions from IP, having ended the lineup close to the 20 feet minimum against the fingertip formation line. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the fingertip line before signalling ready rather than opening the clearance after direction.
texts_at.2: SP stopped close to the fingertip line on the first attempt, with the wingtip clearance sitting near the 20 feet minimum, then recognized it before signalling ready and taxied out a few feet to re-establish a clear margin without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the fingertip line before stopping rather than adjusting it after the first attempt.
texts_at.3: SP lined up on the fingertip line with a clear margin over the 20 feet minimum on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth line up needing a small adjustment after stopping a little close. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm that one line up with the same care the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP stopped close to the fingertip line on the first attempt, with the wingtip clearance sitting near the 20 feet minimum, but recognized this before signalling ready and taxied out a few feet without prompting, re-establishing a clear margin. Confirming the fingertip line before stopping, rather than adjusting it after the first attempt, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady lineup precision on the fingertip formation line.
texts_above.3: SP lined up on the close fingertip formation line on the own half of the runway, with lateral wingtip clearance comfortably above the 20 feet minimum and the fore-aft position matched to the room Number 1 had left, needing no adjustment afterward. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed lineup precision on the fingertip formation line.
texts_above.4: SP established the lineup geometry accurately at the first attempt, holding clearly more than the minimum wingtip clearance and stopping in the exact fore-aft position Number 1's taxi distance allowed, with no repositioning of any kind required. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding lineup precision on the fingertip formation line.

error_modes.label: Aircraft creep and cockpit fixation during the formation run-up

texts.0: SP, due to brakes that were not pumped up before the run-up and attention held inside the cockpit on the engine instruments, did not detect the aircraft creeping forward while both aircraft were stabilized at approximately 30 percent torque. The aircraft crept out of the briefed fore-aft position and ahead of Number 1's wing line with no outside crosscheck at any point of the run-up. IP applied the brakes and repositioned the aircraft before the brake release signal could be given.
texts.1: SP, due to fixating inside the cockpit while checking the engine at approximately 30 percent torque, did not crosscheck outside to detect creep during the run-up. The aircraft moved forward to the limit of the acceptable fore-aft band and was stopped only after the IP called the creep twice. The engine check itself was completed correctly but the outside scan was resumed only on direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that stayed inside the cockpit slightly longer than required while confirming the engine indications, did not detect the start of the forward creep at approximately 30 percent torque. The aircraft moved about half a fuselage length forward of the briefed reference before SP looked out, applied the brakes and re-established the position in good time for the run-up signal. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP pumped up the brakes before the run-up, advanced the PCL smoothly to approximately 30 percent torque and alternated the scan between the engine indications and the outside references. No creep developed and the briefed fore-aft position was held unchanged until brake release. The head nod was given with the aircraft steady in position.
texts.4: SP held the aircraft completely still through the run-up, with the brakes pumped up beforehand and the scan divided so that the engine check never took the eyes off the outside references for more than a moment. The fore-aft position on Number 1 did not move perceptibly at any stage of the run-up. The engine check and the ready signal were completed without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft within the acceptable position band during the run-up, but the scan stayed inside the cockpit for long spells and a small forward creep was allowed to start on more than one occasion. The pattern indicates that the outside crosscheck is being treated as secondary to the engine check rather than being interleaved with it. SP is expected to pump up the brakes before the run-up and to break the instrument scan often enough that creep is detected at its onset.

texts_at.1: SP moved to the limit of the acceptable fore-aft band during the run-up and was stopped only after IP called the creep twice, because the scan stayed inside the cockpit while checking the engine at torque. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to alternate the scan outside during the engine check so creep is not called by IP.
texts_at.2: SP moved about half a fuselage length forward of the briefed reference before looking out, because the scan stayed inside the cockpit slightly longer than required while confirming the engine indications, then applied the brakes and re-established the position without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to break the scan outside sooner during the engine check rather than confirming the indications first.
texts_at.3: SP held the aircraft within the acceptable position band during the run-up on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth needing a small correction after the scan stayed inside a moment longer than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same scan discipline on every run-up that the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP moved about half a fuselage length forward of the briefed reference before looking out, because the scan stayed inside the cockpit slightly longer than required, but applied the brakes and re-established the position without prompting, in good time for the run-up signal. Breaking the scan outside sooner during the engine check, rather than confirming the indications first, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady position discipline during the formation run-up.
texts_above.3: SP pumped up the brakes before the run-up, advanced the PCL smoothly to approximately 30 percent torque and alternated the scan between the engine indications and the outside references, holding the briefed fore-aft position unchanged until brake release. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate position discipline during the formation run-up.
texts_above.4: SP held the aircraft completely still through the run-up, with the brakes pumped up beforehand and the scan divided so the engine check never took the eyes off the outside references for more than a moment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary position discipline during the formation run-up.

error_modes.label: Power push technique and use of the power advantage at brake release

texts.0: SP, due to advancing the PCL to MAX at brake release and leaving it there instead of pulling it back one lever width to approximately 85 percent, did not preserve the power advantage over Number 1's 85 to 95 percent setting as a usable margin. The aircraft accelerated past Number 1 with no reserve left to modulate the position, the airspeed spread opened beyond 20 knots and the fore-aft geometry could not be recovered on the runway. IP retarded the PCL and took control to re-establish spacing from Number 1.
texts.1: SP, due to a power push made in large uncontrolled lever movements rather than smoothly to MAX and back one lever width, did not set a stable power condition for the acceleration. Torque was swung repeatedly between MAX and well below 85 percent, the aircraft oscillated fore and aft to the limit of the acceptable band and the airspeed spread reached about 20 knots. Power was stabilized only after successive verbal corrections from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a power push completed a little after brake release rather than with it, did not have the approximately 85 percent setting established during the first part of the acceleration. The aircraft fell about half a fuselage length aft of the briefed reference and the airspeed spread reached some 14 knots. SP applied the remaining lever width smoothly, regained the position well before rotation and did so without any assistance.
texts.3: SP executed the power push smoothly at brake release, pushing the PCL to MAX and pulling it back one lever width to approximately 85 percent, and then used the remaining advantage in small increments to hold the briefed position. The airspeed spread with Number 1 stayed within 10 knots throughout the acceleration. Power corrections were small and always in the correct direction.
texts.4: SP used the power push technique precisely, so that the approximately 85 percent setting was established with the brakes released and a controllable advantage over Number 1 was available at every stage of the roll. Position corrections were made with fractions of a lever width and were anticipatory, so no perceptible movement developed in the formation geometry. The technique was applied without prompting and with no airspeed excursion.
texts.marginal: SP applied the power push and held the position within acceptable limits, but habitually settled below the approximately 85 percent target and then had to chase the position with a larger addition of power. The trend shows the advantage over Number 1 being given away at brake release and recovered late. SP is expected to set the lever width back from MAX accurately so that the power advantage remains available for small corrections throughout the roll.

texts_at.1: SP held the airspeed spread to about 20 knots, at the tolerance limit, because the power push was made in large uncontrolled lever movements rather than smoothly to MAX and back one lever width, until IP made successive corrections. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to execute the power push in one smooth movement so the spread does not run to the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP let the airspeed spread reach about 14 knots, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the power push was completed a little after brake release rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to execute the power push exactly with brake release rather than a moment after it.
texts_at.3: SP held the airspeed spread within 10 knots throughout the acceleration on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth needing a small correction after the power push lagged brake release by a moment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to execute that one power push with the same timing the first three showed.

texts_above.2: SP let the airspeed spread reach about 14 knots because the power push lagged brake release by a noticeable margin, but recognized the power setting on the torque indication and stabilized the speed without prompting, regaining the briefed position well before rotation. Executing the power push exactly with brake release, rather than a moment after it, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured power push technique at brake release.
texts_above.3: SP executed the power push smoothly at brake release, pushing the PCL to MAX and pulling it back one lever width to approximately 85 percent, holding the airspeed spread within 10 knots with corrections small and always in the correct direction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good power push technique at brake release.
texts_above.4: SP used the power push technique precisely, so the approximately 85 percent setting was established with the brakes released and a controllable advantage over Number 1 was available at every stage, with no airspeed excursion developing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior power push technique at brake release.

error_modes.label: Matching Number 1's pitch attitude at rotation and stacking level

texts.0: SP, due to rotating on his own airspeed indications instead of matching Number 1's pitch attitude, did not lift off with the formation and did not establish the level stack with the anti-collision light in the exhaust. The aircraft ballooned above Number 1 and the split exceeded 350 feet before the gear and flaps were raised, well outside the tolerance. IP took control and repositioned the aircraft into the briefed stack.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch input made independently of Number 1's takeoff attitude, did not match the rotation and did not hold the level stack through the transition to flight. The vertical split reached about 300 feet, at the limit of the tolerance, and the anti-collision light reference was regained only after repeated verbal directions from the IP. Each pitch correction was initiated late.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly delayed pitch input at Number 1's rotation, did not lift off simultaneously with the formation and initially stacked below the briefed reference. The split reached about 200 feet with the anti-collision light seen high on the fuselage rather than in the exhaust. SP re-established the level stack with a small pitch adjustment before the gear and flaps were raised, with no intervention.
texts.3: SP matched Number 1's pitch attitude at rotation and lifted off with the formation, then held the level stack with the anti-collision light in the exhaust until the gear and flaps were raised. The vertical split stayed within 150 feet throughout the transition. Pitch corrections were small and referenced to the visual cues on Number 1 rather than to the flight instruments.
texts.4: SP matched Number 1's pitch attitude exactly at rotation, so that the two aircraft became airborne together with no perceptible change in the formation geometry. The anti-collision light was held in the exhaust throughout the transition and the vertical split remained within a few tens of feet until the gear and flaps were raised. No pitch chasing developed at any point.
texts.marginal: SP matched the rotation and held the stack within standards, but consistently a little high on Number 1, with the anti-collision light seen above the exhaust line and the split reaching 120 to 150 feet. The pattern indicates that pitch is being set from the airspeed and the runway picture rather than from Number 1's attitude. SP is expected to take the pitch cue directly from Number 1 so that the level stack is preserved through the lift off.

texts_at.1: SP held the vertical split to about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, because the pitch input at Number 1's rotation was made independently of the leader's takeoff attitude, until IP made repeated corrections. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match Number 1's pitch attitude directly at rotation rather than correcting the split afterward.
texts_at.2: SP initially stacked below the briefed reference by about 200 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the pitch input at Number 1's rotation was slightly delayed, before re-establishing the level stack with a small pitch adjustment without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the pitch input to Number 1's rotation exactly rather than adjusting the stack afterward.
texts_at.3: SP matched Number 1's pitch attitude and held the vertical split within 150 feet through the transition on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth needing a small correction after a pitch input a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to time that one pitch input as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP initially stacked below the briefed reference by about 200 feet because the pitch input at Number 1's rotation was slightly delayed, but re-established the level stack with a small pitch adjustment without prompting before the gear and flaps were raised. Timing the pitch input to Number 1's rotation exactly, rather than adjusting the stack afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent pitch matching and stack discipline at rotation.
texts_above.3: SP matched Number 1's pitch attitude at rotation and lifted off with the formation, then held the level stack with the anti-collision light in the exhaust until the gear and flaps were raised, keeping the vertical split within 150 feet. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pitch matching and stack discipline at rotation.
texts_above.4: SP matched Number 1's pitch attitude exactly at rotation, so the two aircraft became airborne together with no perceptible change in the formation geometry and the vertical split stayed within a few tens of feet. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding pitch matching and stack discipline at rotation.

error_modes.label: Gear and flap retraction sequencing relative to Number 1

texts.0: SP, due to raising the gear on his own airspeed indication rather than on Number 1's gear beginning to retract, did not respect the rule that Number 2 never raises the gear before Number 1. The aircraft cleaned up first, accelerated ahead of the formation and moved forward of Number 1's wing line with the split still increasing. IP took control to arrest the closure and re-establish the briefed position.
texts.1: SP, due to anticipating the configuration change instead of waiting for Number 1's gear to start moving, selected the gear up at the same instant as Number 1 with the formation only just at the minimum of 110 KIAS. The resulting acceleration drove the position to the limit of the acceptable band and was contained only after verbal directions from the IP. The flap retraction was likewise made on prompting rather than on the observed cue.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that returned to Number 1's gear slightly late while the climb was being established, did not raise the gear immediately after Number 1's gear began to retract. The aircraft carried the drag a few seconds longer and fell about half a fuselage length aft of the briefed position. SP recognized the lag, cleaned up the configuration and regained the position with a measured power addition and no assistance.
texts.3: SP raised the gear and flaps only after the formation was climbing and Number 1's gear had begun to retract, with the formation safely airborne at a minimum of 110 KIAS. The configuration change produced no significant movement in the formation geometry. The after takeoff check was then completed while the visual reference on Number 1 was maintained.
texts.4: SP timed the configuration change precisely on Number 1's gear starting to retract, so that the two aircraft cleaned up in sequence with no perceptible change in position. When a slight overrun developed, SP deliberately delayed the gear retraction to use the drag as a corrective and returned to the briefed position without touching the power. The after takeoff check was completed without any degradation of the visual reference.
texts.marginal: SP kept the retraction sequence correct and the position within standards, but repeatedly moved the gear handle at almost the same moment as Number 1 rather than after Number 1's gear had visibly started to move. The trend is toward anticipating the cue, which leaves no margin if Number 1 delays the retraction. SP is expected to wait for the observed movement of Number 1's gear before selecting the configuration change.

texts_at.1: SP selected the gear up at the same instant as Number 1 with the formation only just at the minimum airspeed, and the resulting acceleration drove the position to the limit of the acceptable band until IP gave verbal direction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to wait for Number 1's gear to visibly start moving before selecting the configuration change.
texts_at.2: SP carried the drag a few seconds longer than Number 1 and fell about half a fuselage length aft of the briefed position, because the scan returned to Number 1's gear slightly late while the climb was being established, then recognized the lag and regained the position with a measured power addition without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to return the scan to Number 1's gear as the climb is established rather than after a lag develops.
texts_at.3: SP raised the gear and flaps only after Number 1's gear began to retract on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth needing a measured power addition after the scan returned a moment late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to time that one retraction as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP carried the drag a few seconds longer than Number 1 and fell about half a fuselage length aft of the briefed position, because the scan returned to Number 1's gear slightly late, but recognized the lag and regained the position with a measured power addition without prompting. Returning the scan to Number 1's gear as the climb is established, rather than after a lag develops, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable gear and flap sequencing relative to Number 1.
texts_above.3: SP raised the gear and flaps only after the formation was climbing and Number 1's gear had begun to retract, with the configuration change producing no significant movement in the formation geometry. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good gear and flap sequencing relative to Number 1.
texts_above.4: SP timed the configuration change precisely on Number 1's gear starting to retract, so the two aircraft cleaned up in sequence with no perceptible change in position, and even deliberately delayed the gear once to use the drag as a corrective. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior gear and flap sequencing relative to Number 1.

error_modes.label: Transition to a separate takeoff when the position cannot be held
error_modes.source: technique:9.42 FORMATION TAKEOFF ABNORMALITIES AND ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to continuing to chase the fore-aft position with the PCL after the aircraft had already overrun Number 1, did not select MAX power and make a separate takeoff and did not maintain the same side of the runway. The aircraft drifted across toward Number 1's half of the runway while still ahead of the formation, with the lateral clearance closing throughout. IP took control, applied MAX power and re-established the aircraft on its own side of the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to persisting with normal power settings after it had become clear that the fore or aft position could not be maintained, did not transition to a separate takeoff in time. MAX power was selected and the same side of the runway held only after the IP directed it, by which point the aircraft was at the limit of the acceptable lateral band. Number 1's subsequent directions were then followed correctly.
texts.2: SP, due to a short delay in accepting that the position was no longer recoverable with normal power, did not select MAX power at the first opportunity when the aircraft overran Number 1. The aircraft continued forward for several seconds before SP applied MAX power, held the same side of the runway and made a separate takeoff. Number 1's directions for the rejoin were followed without any assistance.
texts.3: SP recognized that the position could not be held with normal power settings, selected MAX power and made a separate takeoff while maintaining the same side of the runway throughout. Runway alignment on his own half was held within the tolerance and Number 1's directions for the rejoin were followed correctly. The transition was made without hesitation.
texts.4: SP identified the developing overrun early, selected MAX power and made a separate takeoff before the geometry became uncomfortable, with the aircraft held precisely on its own side of the runway. The intention was passed clearly and the aircraft was flown accurately on the departure heading while awaiting Number 1's direction for the rejoin. Aircraft control and the visual picture on Number 1 were never in doubt.
texts.marginal: SP made the separate takeoff and held the correct side of the runway within standards, but only after working the throttle against a position that was already lost. The pattern indicates a reluctance to abandon the formation takeoff while any chance of holding position appears to remain. SP is expected to make the decision at the point where normal power settings are no longer sufficient, so that the separate takeoff begins from a comfortable geometry.

texts_at.1: SP selected MAX power and held the same side of the runway only after IP directed it, at the limit of the acceptable lateral band, because normal power settings were persisted with after the fore or aft position could no longer be maintained. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select MAX power at the first sign the position cannot be held rather than after direction.
texts_at.2: SP continued forward for several seconds before applying MAX power, having taken a short delay accepting that the position was no longer recoverable with normal power, then held the same side of the runway and made a separate takeoff without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize the loss of position as promptly as the decision to select MAX power was carried out.
texts_at.3: SP recognized that the position could not be held and selected MAX power for a separate takeoff on three of the four occasions, the fourth decision coming a few seconds later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that one decision as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.2: SP continued forward for several seconds before applying MAX power, having taken a short delay accepting that the position was no longer recoverable, but then held the same side of the runway and made a separate takeoff without prompting, following Number 1's directions correctly. Recognizing the loss of position as promptly as the decision to select MAX power was carried out, rather than after a delay, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured decision timing for a separate takeoff.
texts_above.3: SP recognized that the position could not be held with normal power settings, selected MAX power and made a separate takeoff while maintaining the same side of the runway throughout, with Number 1's directions for the rejoin followed correctly. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise decision timing for a separate takeoff.
texts_above.4: SP identified the developing overrun early, selected MAX power and made a separate takeoff before the geometry became uncomfortable, with the aircraft held precisely on its own side of the runway throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate decision timing for a separate takeoff.

error_modes.label: Crosscheck of engine instruments and airspeed when falling behind Number 1
error_modes.source: technique:9.42 FORMATION TAKEOFF ABNORMALITIES AND ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to attention held entirely on Number 1 while the aircraft was falling behind, did not crosscheck the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator and therefore had no basis to choose between an abort and a separate takeoff. The aircraft continued the roll well aft of any usable position with an unassessed engine condition and no decision made. IP took control and directed the required action.
texts.1: SP, due to an outside reference held on Number 1 to the exclusion of the cockpit indications, did not crosscheck the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator as the aircraft fell behind. The crosscheck was made only after the IP directed it, at the limit of the runway distance available to act, and the decision to continue as a separate takeoff was consequently late. The engine indications were normal when finally checked.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief hesitation over whether to look inside while the position was degrading, did not crosscheck the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator immediately when the aircraft began to fall behind. Several seconds were lost before SP checked the indications, confirmed normal engine operation and continued as a separate takeoff. The decision was made in time and without any assistance.
texts.3: SP recognized that the aircraft was falling behind, crosschecked the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator without delay and, having confirmed no problem, continued as a separate takeoff and rejoined after becoming safely airborne. Aircraft control and runway alignment were maintained throughout the crosscheck. The reasoning was stated clearly afterwards.
texts.4: SP detected the aft drift at its onset, crosschecked the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator in a single deliberate scan and reached the continue or abort decision with ample runway remaining. The crosscheck did not interrupt the outside picture on Number 1 or the directional control of the aircraft. The separate takeoff and subsequent rejoin were flown exactly as directed.
texts.marginal: SP crosschecked the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator and reached the correct decision within the time available, but only once the aircraft was clearly out of position rather than at the first sign of the aft drift. The trend suggests the cockpit indications are consulted as a last resort rather than as the basis of the decision. SP is expected to crosscheck as soon as the aircraft starts to fall behind, so that the abort or continue decision is made with more runway in hand.

texts_at.1: SP made the crosscheck of the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator only after IP directed it, at the limit of the runway distance available to act, because attention was held entirely on Number 1 while the aircraft was falling behind. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to crosscheck the instruments as soon as the aircraft begins to fall behind rather than needing it directed.
texts_at.2: SP lost several seconds before checking the indications, because of a brief hesitation over whether to look inside while the position was degrading, then confirmed normal engine operation and continued as a separate takeoff without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to crosscheck the indications immediately the aircraft begins to fall behind rather than hesitating first.
texts_at.3: SP crosschecked the engine instruments and the airspeed indicator without delay when the aircraft began to fall behind on three of the four occasions, the fourth crosscheck coming a few seconds later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that one crosscheck as prompt as the first three.
